text:
For the Camporini deadlift, you can ignore that one.

For the alternating dumbbell or barbell deadlifts, I'm standing there with dumbbells in my hands or a barbell, and I take one half step back. I can deadlift essentially at a staggered stance on one leg, then I switch legs and deadlift on the other one, and then I switch legs and continually alternate doing deadlifts on each leg. I can save a lot of time by doing alternating dumbbell or barbell single-leg or unilateral deadlifts.

For the single-leg getups, you're sitting on a box, a bench, or a chair, and you put one foot forward and try to stand up with that one foot. The other foot is just helping you by touching the ground for balance, but essentially you're getting up with one leg at a time. You can use the other foot for balance, or you could just keep that other foot off the ground completely. Essentially, almost like an assisted pistol or a box pistol, it behaves the same way.

For the low dumbbell squats, you need to put both dumbbells on your sides by your legs, and you squat down with your arms hanging down on the dumbbells. Both arms are at your side, keeping the dumbbells down. Not a goblet, not racked at the top, or anything like that.

For the con row, you have two kettlebells on the ground. You stand right in front of them, open up your legs, hinge down, row them off the ground, and then put them back on the ground. Usually, this is for people that have some type of shoulder pain or back pain in order to row and to make sure that they get stronger in their hinging positions, but it's not really advanced. It doesn't really create a lot of stimulus, so I wouldn't really give a lot of importance to it.

The strap rotating in and out, you can take that one away, doesn't matter. The pull under is really called a pull over. If you're doing it on a cable machine with your lats, you're doing a lat pull over. That's what I mean by that.
